formation.title: The Rebirth of Carthage
formation.text:
The ancient city rises again. Where once the Phoenician traders built a thalassocracy that rivaled Rome itself, a new Carthage now commands the crossroads of the Mediterranean. The cothon harbors of old may lie in ruins, but the spirit of Baal Hammon and the legacy of Hannibal Barca stir in the hearts of our people.

Two visions compete for the soul of this reborn nation. Shall we reclaim the seas as our ancestors did: masters of trade, shipbuilding, and maritime dominion from the Pillars of Hercules to the shores of Sicily? Or shall we forge a continental empire worthy of the Barcid generals, drawing upon the diverse peoples of Africa and Iberia as Carthage always did: not through citizen armies but through the disciplined strength of recruited nations?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Command the seas as our ancestors did

modifiers.name: Punic Thalassocracy
modifiers.text: Carthage commands the Mediterranean through the same instruments that built the original Punic empire: unmatched seamanship, far-reaching trade networks, and the commercial wealth they generate.

options.text: Build an empire worthy of the Barcids

modifiers.name: Punic Imperium
modifiers.text: In the tradition of Hamilcar and Hannibal, the new Carthage builds its power through military excellence: recruiting the finest warriors from subject peoples and forging them into a disciplined instrument of conquest.

advances.name: Cult of Baal Hammon
advances.text: The restoration of the Tophet as a center of Punic worship, honoring the ancient gods Baal Hammon and Tanit through ritual and devotion.

event.title: Consecration of the Tophet
event.text:
At the ancient precinct of Salambo, where thousands of stelae still stand inscribed to Baal Hammon and Tanit, the sacred flames burn once more. The Tophet (that most sacred and most debated of Carthaginian institutions) has been restored as the spiritual heart of the reborn nation.

Whether the urns once held the ashes of sacrificed firstborn or merely stillborn children given to the gods, the Tophet's power as a symbol of Punic devotion is beyond question. The triangular sign of Tanit, carved into fresh stone, declares to all who pass: Carthage remembers its gods.

options.text: The gods of Carthage watch over us

modifiers.name: Blessing of Baal Hammon
modifiers.text: The ancient gods of Carthage smile upon the restored Tophet. Religious devotion strengthens the bonds of Punic society.

advances.name: Sacred Band Tradition
advances.text: Drawing on the legacy of Carthage's elite citizen soldiers, the Sacred Band, who fought as heavy infantry in the ancient phalanx formations.

advances.name: Tyrian Purple
advances.text: The revival of the ancient Phoenician craft of extracting purple dye from murex sea snails, producing the legendary Tyrian purple cloth that was once worth more than gold.

advances.name: Triple Wall Fortifications
advances.text: The massive triple-walled defenses that once protected Carthage (three concentric walls with stabling for war elephants and barracks within) inspire a new generation of fortification.

advances.name: Lettered Timbers
advances.text: Carthaginian shipwrights painted a letter on every rib and matched it on the keel, so a hull went together in the order its parts were marked. Yards that work this way build war galleys in batches and replace a lost fleet in a season.

event.title: The Lettered Timbers
event.text:
In the yards the ribs lie stacked in rows, each with a Punic letter painted on it, and the same letters run along the keel to show where every rib belongs. A crew that has never built a warship can follow the marks. A Carthaginian galley lost off Marsala around 241 BC still carries them.

Rome learned what the method was worth. Early in the first war it took a stranded Carthaginian warship as its pattern, and Pliny says the fleet built on that pattern was afloat sixty days after the trees were felled.

The method is ours again. Hulls are cut and lettered through the winter and put together when the fleet calls for them. The first war galleys built this way are on the slips.

modifiers.name: Punic Engineering Legacy
modifiers.text: Parts are cut and lettered ahead of need and assembled in order. The habit spreads from the shipyards to every building site in Carthage.

advances.name: Numidian Cavalry Tradition
advances.text: The recruitment and training of Numidian light horsemen who ride without bridle, hurling javelins with deadly accuracy: the finest light cavalry in the ancient Mediterranean.

advances.name: Phoenician Glassmaking
advances.text: The Phoenicians were legendary glassmakers, and Carthage inherits their techniques, producing translucent glass vessels, colored beads, and decorative wares prized across the Mediterranean.

advances.name: Council of Elders
advances.text: The Carthaginian senate (the Council of Elders) governed through deliberation and consensus, providing stable administration and careful statecraft.

advances.name: Libyan Infantry Reforms
advances.text: Reorganization of the subject Libyan infantry into disciplined spear formations, equipped with bronze helmets and aspis shields in the manner of the old Punic heavy infantry.

advances.name: Naval Ram Tactics
advances.text: The development of the quinquereme (the five-banked warship that was Carthage's signature vessel), armed with a devastating bronze ram at the prow.

advances.name: Punic Literary Tradition
advances.text: When Carthage fell, Rome gave its libraries away to the kings of Numidia. Punic was still spoken and written in Africa five centuries later. The script returns to use, and the presses of Carthage print in it.

advances.name: Carthaginian Diplomacy
advances.text: Carthage's diplomatic tradition: a network of treaties, trade agreements, and intelligence networks that once spanned from the Tin Islands to the coast of West Africa.

advances.name: Royal Purple Monopoly
advances.text: State control over the lucrative purple dye trade, ensuring Carthage's monopoly on the most prestigious luxury commodity in the Mediterranean world.

advances.name: Mediterranean Naval Dominance
advances.text: Carthaginian mastery of the central Mediterranean, controlling the sea lanes between Africa, Sicily, and Sardinia through superior seamanship and galley tactics.

advances.name: Punic Urban Planning
advances.text: The systematic layout of Carthaginian cities: regular street grids, multi-story insulae, sophisticated drainage, and careful zoning of commercial and residential districts.

advances.name: Mercenary Army Reforms
advances.text: The restructuring of Carthage's polyglot mercenary forces into organized contingents with standardized logistics, drawing upon Iberian, Gallic, Libyan, and Numidian recruits.

advances.name: Punic Military Reform
advances.text: A comprehensive restructuring of the Carthaginian army, moving beyond reliance on mercenary bands toward a professional standing force with standardized equipment and training.

advances.name: Legacy of the Barcids
advances.text: The memory of the Barcid dynasty (Hamilcar, Hasdrubal, and above all Hannibal) inspires a new era of naval ambition and strategic boldness.

advances.name: Punic Institutional Revival
advances.text: The systematic restoration of Carthaginian administrative institutions (the suffetes, the treasury, the census, and the courts), providing a framework for modern governance.

advances.name: Punic Siege Engineering
advances.text: Drawing on the engineering traditions that built Carthage's massive fortifications, Punic siege experts develop techniques to both construct and breach the mightiest walls.

advances.name: Punic Constitutional Reform
advances.text: Aristotle praised the Carthaginian constitution as among the finest in the ancient world. Its revival establishes a balanced system of magistrates, councils, and popular assemblies.

advances.name: Carthaginian Cultural Renaissance
advances.text: A flowering of Punic arts, scholarship, and literature, drawing on the rich heritage of Phoenician and Carthaginian civilization to create a distinctive cultural identity.

advances.name: Modern Punic Fleet
advances.text: The transformation of the Carthaginian navy from galley-based warfare to modern ship construction, while retaining the seamanship and tactical traditions of the ancient fleet.

advances.name: Neo-Punic Industry
advances.text: The industrial development of Carthaginian territories, building on centuries of craft expertise in metalworking, glassmaking, textile production, and agricultural processing.

destiny.name: Destiny of Carthage
destiny.text: The foundations of reborn Carthage are secure. From this base of stability, a great destiny beckons, but which destiny shall it be?

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of Carthage
event.text:
Carthage stands reborn, its foundations secure and its people united. The ancient city that once commanded half the Mediterranean now faces a choice that will define its future for centuries to come.

The suffetes and the Council of Elders debate endlessly. Some point to the harbors, the cothons, the merchant fleets: the instruments that built Carthaginian power in the first place. Others invoke the memory of the Barcid generals, who proved that Carthage could match any land power in open battle.

The destiny of Carthage awaits.

options.text: Our destiny is written in the stars

destiny.name: Command of the Sardinian Sea
destiny.text: Secure Sardinia and Corsica to dominate the central Mediterranean. Control these island bastions and fill the treasury to fund further expansion. Requires choosing the Thalassocratic path.

conditions.text: The path of the Thalassocracy
Own Cagliari, or a subject owns it
Own Ajaccio, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: Command of the Sardinian Sea
event.text:
The islands of Sardinia and Corsica (those ancient prizes over which Carthage and Rome first came to blows) are ours once more. The Sardinian Sea, that vital corridor between Africa and Europe, is now a Punic lake.

From Cagliari and Ajaccio, our merchant fleets can reach any port in the western Mediterranean within days. The island fortresses that once served as stepping stones for Roman conquest now serve as bastions of Punic commerce.

destiny.name: The Pillars of Hercules
destiny.text: Command the strait where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic. Seize Cadiz, Gibraltar, and Cartagena to control the western sea lanes and the ancient Punic trade routes.

conditions.text: Own Cádiz, or a subject owns it
Own Gibraltar, or a subject owns it
Own Cartagena, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Pillars of Hercules
event.text:
The ancient boundary stones of the known world stand under Punic authority. Cadiz (Gadir, as the Phoenicians called it) was the oldest colony in the west, founded before Carthage itself. Gibraltar, the rock that guards the passage between seas, is ours.

Cartagena (New Carthage, Hasdrubal's capital in Iberia) completes the chain. Every ship that passes between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean must now reckon with Punic power. The question is whether to turn outward toward the vast ocean, or inward to master the trade of the inner sea.

options.text: Look beyond the Pillars to the Atlantic

modifiers.name: Gateway to the Atlantic
modifiers.text: Command of the Pillars of Hercules opens the vast Atlantic to Punic exploration, extending Carthage's diplomatic and naval reach beyond the ancient world.

options.text: Master the commerce of the inner sea

modifiers.name: Merchant Princes of the Mediterranean
modifiers.text: The wealthiest merchants of the Mediterranean converge on Punic ports, offering favorable credit and strengthening relations, though the comfort of prosperity dulls military preparedness.

destiny.name: Mare Nostrum
destiny.text: Make the entire Mediterranean a Punic lake. Command Genoa, Alexandria, and Crete (the three corners of Mediterranean commerce) and raise Carthage itself to twice the city it was, as befits the greatest harbour of the western sea.

conditions.text: Own Genoa, or a subject owns it
Own Alexandria, or a subject owns it
Own Candia, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
We own Tunis, the site of Carthage, and its development is at least 62

event.title: Mare Nostrum
event.text:
From Genoa to Alexandria, from Crete to the Pillars of Hercules, the Mediterranean is a Punic sea. The dream that Rome achieved through legions and roads, Carthage has accomplished through ships and trade: a commercial empire spanning three continents.

The harbors of Genoa funnel the wealth of Europe. The granaries and workshops of Alexandria channel the riches of the East. The harbors of Crete command the sea lanes between them all. Carthage sits at the center, the spider in a web of commerce that makes the old Roman mare nostrum seem parochial by comparison.

This is the Punic thalassocracy fulfilled: not through the sword, but through the ledger and the sail.

modifiers.name: Punic Dominion
modifiers.text: The Mediterranean basin falls under a unified Punic administration, with subject peoples gradually absorbed into Carthaginian civic life.

modifiers.name: Queen of the Sea
modifiers.text: Carthage presides over the greatest trade network the Mediterranean has ever known, its merchant agents doubling as an unrivaled intelligence network, though such mastery breeds complacency.

destiny.name: African Hegemony
destiny.text: Secure dominion over western North Africa by conquering Fez and Tangier. Build the army that will carry Punic ambitions beyond Africa. Requires choosing the Barcid Imperium path.

conditions.text: The path of the Punic Imperium
Own Fez, or a subject owns it
Own Tangier, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: African Hegemony
event.text:
The western reaches of North Africa bow to Punic authority. Fez, the ancient capital of Morocco, and Tangier, the gateway to the strait, are now Carthaginian possessions. The Berber and Arab peoples of the Maghreb serve under the banner of the new Punic empire, just as the Numidians and Libyans once served under the Barcids.

With Africa secured, the army grows stronger by the day. The diverse peoples of the continent provide cavalry, infantry, and specialists of every kind. The path northward beckons.

options.text: Africa is ours. Now look north

destiny.name: The Iberian Campaign
destiny.text: Cross the strait as Hamilcar once did. Conquer Granada, Cordoba, and Sevilla, the rich cities of southern Iberia that funded the original Barcid campaigns against Rome.

conditions.text: Own Granada, or a subject owns it
Own Córdoba, or a subject owns it
Own Sevilla, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Iberian Campaign
event.text:
Hamilcar Barca crossed into Iberia to rebuild Carthaginian power after the First Punic War. His son Hannibal launched the greatest military campaign of antiquity from these same shores. Now a new generation of Punic soldiers stands in Granada, Cordoba, and Sevilla: the rich cities of Andalusia that once funded Barcid ambitions.

The veterans of this campaign are hardened by siege and battle. The question is whether to forge them into a professional elite or to open the ranks wider, drawing on the vast manpower of our African territories.

modifiers.name: Iberian Veterans
modifiers.text: The veterans of the Iberian campaign form the professional core of the Punic army, rapidly reinforced and quickly mustered, though the hard campaigning takes its toll on the troops.

options.text: Recruit from our vast African domains

modifiers.name: African Recruits
modifiers.text: The vast African territories supply strong garrisons and the confidence to wage aggressive wars, though the strain of maintaining such forces across the continent fuels rising prices.

destiny.name: Hannibal ante Portas
destiny.text: Finish what Hannibal could not. Take Rome and Naples, the heart of the ancient enemy, and hold half of Campania, the land that went over to him after Cannae. With the Eternal City in Punic hands, the Mediterranean world bows to Carthage at last.

conditions.text: Own Rome, or a subject owns it
Own Naples, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 75
Prestige at least 75
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least 50% of the locations in Campania

event.title: Hannibal ante Portas
event.text:
Hannibal ad portas: 'Hannibal is at the gates!' The cry that once terrorized Roman mothers into silence now echoes through the streets of the Eternal City itself. Rome has fallen. Naples has fallen. The ancient enemy that razed Carthage to the ground and sowed its fields with salt has been brought to its knees.

What Hannibal could not achieve with his elephants and genius, what Hasdrubal could not accomplish with reinforcements from Iberia, the new Carthage has done. The Punic eagle perches where the Roman wolf once stood.

The world holds its breath. What will the new masters of Rome build upon the ruins of the old?

options.text: Let Punic triumph echo through the ages

modifiers.name: Punic Triumph
modifiers.text: The fall of Rome crowns Carthage as the undisputed master of the Mediterranean, granting unmatched leverage in peace negotiations while plundered wealth sustains the army.

options.text: Build a new order from this conquest

modifiers.name: New Punic Order
modifiers.text: With Rome fallen, Carthage builds a new political order: a multiethnic empire that embraces diverse faiths and converts subject peoples to Punic civic life.

units.name: Sacred Band
units.text: Elite citizen heavy infantry drawn from Carthage's wealthiest families, trained from youth in phalanx warfare. The Sacred Band serves as the backbone of the citizen army.

units.name: Numidian Light Horse
units.text: Swift Numidian cavalrymen who ride without bridle or saddle, hurling javelins with lethal accuracy before wheeling away. Masters of pursuit and desert warfare.

units.name: Punic War Galley
units.text: A purpose-built warship in the Carthaginian tradition, faster and more maneuverable than standard galleys, designed for ramming and boarding actions.

units.name: Libyan Spearmen
units.text: Disciplined African infantry armed with long spears, bronze helmets, and round shields. These subject soldiers form the reliable core of Carthaginian land armies.

units.name: Punic Quinquereme
units.text: The mighty quinquereme: a five-banked warship armed with a devastating bronze ram. The signature vessel of Carthaginian naval power, capable of dominating any sea battle.

buildings.name: Tophet Shrine
buildings.text: A sacred precinct dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, where stelae are erected and offerings made according to ancient Punic religious tradition.

buildings.name: Punic Shipyard
buildings.text: A protected harbor facility built on cothon principles: covered berths, repair docks, and launching ramps that allow rapid construction and maintenance of warships.

buildings.name: Punic Glassworks
buildings.text: A workshop specializing in the ancient Phoenician art of glassmaking, producing colored vessels, beads, and decorative glass prized throughout the Mediterranean trade networks.

buildings.name: Punic Dye Works
buildings.text: A coastal facility for the extraction and processing of murex purple dye: the legendary Tyrian purple that was once the monopoly of Phoenician merchants.

buildings.name: Punic Citadel
buildings.text: A massive fortification inspired by the triple walls of ancient Carthage, with thick stone ramparts, deep ditches, and internal chambers for supply storage.

buildings.name: Punic Emporium
buildings.text: A fortified coastal trading post in the Carthaginian tradition, where merchants from across the Mediterranean gather to exchange goods under the protection of Punic law.

buildings.name: Punic Fondouk
buildings.text: A fortified trading house in the Carthaginian tradition, providing lodging, warehousing, and commercial space for the diverse merchants of the Mediterranean trade networks.

buildings.name: Suffete Court
buildings.text: The seat of the suffetes (the paired magistrates who governed Carthage), restored as a center of civic administration, justice, and public record-keeping.

buildings.name: Grand Cothon Emporium
buildings.text: A monumental harbor-market complex combining the ancient cothon shipbuilding tradition with the commercial infrastructure of a great Mediterranean trading house.

buildings.name: Barcid Military Academy
buildings.text: An officer training school inspired by the strategic genius of Hamilcar, Hasdrubal, and Hannibal Barca, educating the next generation of Punic commanders.

list.name: Andalusi Secretaries
list.text: When Valencia fell in 1238 and Seville in 1248, the secretaries of al-Andalus crossed to Tunis, and the Hafsid sultans gave them the chancery. Ibn al-Abbar of Valencia drafted the sultan's letters from 1240. The Banu Khaldun of Seville served the court for a century, and Ibn Khaldun began his career there in 1352, writing the sultan's mark of validation on decrees. The newcomers reorganised the administration on the model of Cordoba and Seville and became the sultans' closest advisers. The Almohad shaykhs and the tribes of the interior resented them, and in the next century scribes of Almohad descent took many of the offices back.

list.name: Qadi al-Jama'a
list.text: The chief Maliki qadi of Ifriqiya, seated in Tunis. The Maghrib preferred the title qadi al-jama'a (judge of the community) to the eastern qadi al-qudat, reflecting the Maliki tradition of communal rather than centralised judicial hierarchy. Notable holders elsewhere in the Almoravid and Almohad realms included Ibn Rushd al-Jadd and Qadi Iyad of Ceuta. The office arbitrated contracts, inheritance, and personal status, and through its appellate authority steadily displaced the customary law of the Berber and Arab confederations.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Diwan al-Bahr
list.text: The Hafsid maritime bureau, the customs and revenue office at Tunis, La Goulette, and Bougie that taxed the goods landed by the Saharan caravans and traded through the European funduqs. Genoese, Pisan, Catalan, and Venetian merchants leased their warehouses from the diwan and paid its tithes (ushur) under standing treaties such as that of 1323. The maritime bureau registered every harbour due and every concession, underwriting the prosperity of the 14th and 15th centuries.

conditions.text: Owns Tunis

list.name: Ribat Network
list.text: The chain of fortified frontier-monasteries (Sousse, Monastir, Tit, the Almohad Ribat al-Fath at Salé, and Ribat Taza) that combined garrison duty with religious devotion. The murabitun who manned them committed to perpetual vigilance against Christian raids and Bedouin incursions, earning baraka through frontier service. By the 13th century many ribats had become hubs of the proto-Sufi turuq, fusing warrior and ascetic ideals at modest cost to the central treasury but at the price of a militant religious establishment uneasy with the cosmopolitan trade of the coastal cities.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Ta'ife Reisi
list.text: The corsair captains' guild, formalised by Hayreddin Barbarossa after his consolidation of Algiers in 1518 and adopted in turn by Tunis and Tripoli. The reises licensed by the regency divan brought captives, cargo, and ransom revenue to the treasury, while their council (the ta'ifa) elected its own kapudan-rais and ran the corso fleet as an autonomous service. By the seventeenth century the captain class had eclipsed the old tribal aristocracy in the political life of the Barbary regencies.
